Way better than the first game. Dark souls mixed with Destiny. 

Tons of guns, tons of builds, tons of replay value.

First of all, let's get some basics out of the way. This is a "Souls-like" game, but with guns. There are lots of experiences in the game that will brutalize your character when you are new to them. This means you will likely die a *lot*, but dying never costs you anything but time. On death you reset to your most recent visited checkpoint with all loot, XP, etc. retained. Visiting a checkpoint restocks all your ammo and abilities, but also resets all the standard enemies on all maps, so it's not something you want to do willy-nilly.

Like many Souls-like games, there is a lot of puzzle solving. Sometimes those puzzles are "where do I best shoot this foe?" More meaningful puzzles relate to unlocking the path through the current objective as well as finding new, better gear. If you don't enjoy searching every possible nook and cranny, and questioning every odd-looking thing to see if you can interact with it, you likely won't achieve peak build potential for your character(s) in this game.

I'm gonna be frank here - the puzzles / clue searching can be [i]incredibly[/i] obtuse. Not a majority of them, but some rather important ones are. The Ur example is probably how you unlock the Engineer archetype. This all means a search engine is probably going to be your friend in this game, even if you like trying to solve / locate most of the things yourself. I seriously have no idea how some of these things were found originally, at least unless it was with a mod of some kind.

Building your character is kind of complicated, honestly, and if you are not a min/maxer willing to read up on how things work on-line, you again probably will never reach peak potential. The game itself is very little help here - it gives you numbers in fairly significant detail, but doesn't tell you how they are actually used. (Other people have figured it out for you though.)

This game is deeply re-playable. Once you complete a "biome" (one of the major map continuity areas - a.k.a. "worlds") you can revisit it in adventure mode. Adventure mode is distinct from the main campaign mode, but your loot and progress carry over between them. This can be important, because the areas you visit in each biome are randomized. Even the same location can be laid out differently between visits, meaning different puzzles and related loot are on offer. So once you finish a biome in the main campaign mode, you may want to re-run it to find things you missed or that just weren't even in the version you "rolled" your first time through.

You can also re-roll the main campaign. There are progressive difficulties on offer too, so you can challenge even an advanced character.

Finally, you can stack multiple archetypes on a single character. You don't have to re-roll. Two archetypes can be active at a time, but the core "traits" of each unlocked AT you get to level 10 (the max) will remain available for you to rank up even when the archetype is not active. For example, the Medic AT has a trait that boosts healing effectiveness. When the Medic is active at level 10, that trait is automatically maxed out. But if Medic is not active, as long as you got Medic to level 10, the trait is available for you to add points to.

A lot of people will play this game online, but you don't need to. A small subset of loot puzzles strictly require at least two people to obtain, but this is not typical, and while more people with balanced archetypes surely makes the game easier, it's not needed. I played the game entirely solo. If you do what I did, though, consider unlocking a medic early. They're not the best solo AT as neither their damage nor durability are amazing, but they're definitely capable of soloing, and a Medic is highly complimentary 2nd class to one of the tougher or damage-focused ATs.

If you liked Remnant: From the Ashes (R:FtA), you will [i]probably[/i] like Remnant 2. Gameplay is close enough to be familiar, but different enough to be somewhat annoying at first. The core gameplay loop is harder, in my opinion. You are swarmed by foes way more often, and drawing aggro from any one thing frequently pulls a wave of foes.

The story is a direct continuation of that from R:FtA, but delayed a couple of decades. The world building is interesting and fairly deep, but leaves a lot of open questions. The worlds you visit are often extremely dark and messed up, and I often found myself really wondering about the how, exactly, they got that way. You usually get an overall answer, but not a lot of specifics.

This game can make use of a high-end PC / GPU, It seems mostly GPU-dependent - my CPU is not stressed while I play. Loading maps does seem extremely I/O intensive, but that is front-loaded and won't hurt you as you run around a map. If you run it on max settings and don't have a decent PC, you will probably impact your ability to play. You need decent aim speed to survive, especially early on, and if your FPS takes a dive, your aim is going to suck. I have a modestly decent spec PC (Core 17-13700K, 64GB RAM) and a somewhat old GPU (RTX 3060TI) and I needed to turn most of my settings to "Low" to have a FPS I was comfortable with. Despite this, the game still looks good.

This game is beautiful in an often desolate and / or horrible way. The attention to detail is truly impressive in my opinion. The visual continuity with the earlier Remnant: From the Ashes is also highly impressive. It feels like the same world(s).

The sound track is, in my opinion, amazing. It's incredibly atmospheric and I love having it on.

The voice acting is very good.
